title: SQL Server Data Types
description: Understand the families of SQL Server data types — exact numerics, strings, dates, binary — and choose the right type for each column.

data.text: Every column in every table has a data type — it tells SQL Server what kind of data the column holds: integers, text, dates, or binary data. Choosing the right type saves disk space, prevents invalid data, and helps queries run faster.
The five families of data types

data.text: Exact numerics store whole numbers and precise decimals without rounding errors. Use these for IDs, counts, prices, and anywhere precision matters.

data.title: DECIMAL vs. FLOAT for prices
data.text: Never use FLOAT for prices — binary floating point cannot exactly represent values like 0.10, leading to rounding errors. Use DECIMAL(p,s) instead, e.g., DECIMAL(10,2) for 10 total digits with 2 after the decimal point.

rows: Fixed-length codes like country codes or state IDs
Most text of known max length — names, addresses
Unicode text — always prefer over VARCHAR for text

data.text: The 'N' prefix (NCHAR, NVARCHAR, NTEXT) stores Unicode, so it can hold accented characters, emojis, and non-Latin scripts. VARCHAR is fine for ASCII-only data like codes, but for user-facing text like names and addresses, prefer NVARCHAR.

data.title: Use DATETIME2 over DATETIME
data.text: The older DATETIME type only goes to 1753 and has 3 ms precision. For any new project, use DATETIME2 or DATE — they align with the SQL standard, have a much wider range, and higher precision.

rows: A globally unique identifier (GUID) — 36 characters like '5959-...

data.title: A realistic table definition
data.code:
CREATE TABLE production.products (
    product_id    INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
    product_name  NVARCHAR(255)   NOT NULL,
    list_price    DECIMAL(10,2)   NOT NULL,
    model_year    SMALLINT,
    is_discontinued BIT           DEFAULT 0,
    created_at    DATETIME2       DEFAULT GETDATE()
);

data.title: Sizing VARCHAR columns
data.text: VARCHAR(n) reserves space only for the actual characters stored, up to n. Setting n too high (like VARCHAR(255) for a 2-char state code) wastes a tiny bit of metadata but doesn't reserve full space. For fixed-width codes, use CHAR(n) instead.

data.title: Quick reference
points: Use INT for most IDs and counts; BIGINT only for very large numbers
Use DECIMAL(p,s) for money and prices — never FLOAT
Use NVARCHAR for user-facing text; VARCHAR for ASCII codes and names
Use DATE, DATETIME2, or TIME — avoid the old DATETIME type
Use BIT for booleans (0/1 flags), UNIQUEIDENTIFIER for GUIDs
